title: 1 Kings 6:14–22
context: 1 Kings 6:14–22 describes the interior. The walls are lined with cedar carved with buds and open flowers, the floor with cypress, and no stone is visible. At the back is the inner sanctuary, the most holy place, a cube of twenty cubits prepared for the ark of the LORD’s covenant and overlaid with pure gold, with gold chains across its front and a gold-covered altar. A cubit is about 18 inches. Both traditions read the measurements and materials as expressing the holiness and glory of the place where God chose to put his name, without making the details a point of theological disagreement.

verses.text: So Solomon built the house and finished it.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon builds the house and finishes it. Arminians see the repeated statement of completion as emphasizing that Solomon carried out the work, returning to the building account after the LORD’s word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and see the narrator resuming the account after the covenant word. Both traditions read the verse as a transition to the description of the interior, which shows the glory of the house.

verses.text: He built the walls of the house within with boards of cedar; from the floor of the house to the walls of the ceiling, he covered them on the inside with wood. He covered the floor of the house with cypress boards.
verses.arminianNotes: He lines the walls of the house with cedar from floor to ceiling and covers the floor with cypress. Arminian readers see costly materials used throughout the interior, showing honor for the LORD’s house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that wood covered all the stone inside. Both traditions read the verse as part of a description that shows the beauty and care given to the place of God’s presence.

verses.text: He built twenty cubits of the back part of the house with boards of cedar from the floor to the ceiling. He built this within, for an inner sanctuary, even for the most holy place.
verses.arminianNotes: He builds twenty cubits at the back of the house with cedar boards, as an inner sanctuary, the most holy place. Arminians see the most holy place set apart within the house, following the pattern of the tabernacle (Exodus 26:33).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and see the most holy place as the center of the temple, where God’s presence was especially associated with the ark. Both traditions read the verse in light of Hebrews 9, which uses the most holy place to explain Christ’s work.

verses.text: In front of the temple sanctuary was forty cubits long.
verses.arminianNotes: The main hall in front of the inner sanctuary is forty cubits long. Arminian readers see the description of the main room, where daily worship took place, distinct from the inner sanctuary that was set apart.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that the main hall and inner sanctuary together make up the sixty cubits of 6:2. Both traditions treat the verse as architectural description without theological contrast.

verses.text: There was cedar on the house within, carved with buds and open flowers. All was cedar. No stone was visible.
verses.arminianNotes: The cedar inside is carved with buds and open flowers, all cedar, with no stone visible. Arminians see beauty and life in the carvings, showing that God’s house was meant to be both holy and beautiful.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree. Many see the plant imagery as recalling a garden and possibly Eden, though the text does not say so directly. Both traditions offer that connection with caution and read the verse as celebrating the beauty of God’s dwelling.

verses.text: He prepared an inner sanctuary in the middle of the house within, to set the ark of the LORD’s covenant there.
verses.arminianNotes: He prepares the inner sanctuary in the middle of the house to set the ark of the LORD’s covenant there. Arminian readers see the ark as the center of the whole project, since the house exists to give the covenant symbol of God’s presence a permanent place.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as the theological center of the description. Both traditions note that the ark, with the covenant inside it (1 Kings 8:9), ties the temple to God’s covenant with Israel.

verses.text: Within the inner sanctuary was twenty cubits in length, and twenty cubits in width, and twenty cubits in its height. He overlaid it with pure gold. He covered the altar with cedar.
verses.arminianNotes: The inner sanctuary is twenty cubits long, wide, and high, overlaid with pure gold, and the altar is covered with cedar. Arminians see the perfect cube shape as a sign of completeness and holiness, though the text does not explain it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that some connect the cube with the city in Revelation 21:16, offered as a possible link rather than a certainty. Both traditions read the gold and the shape as expressing the holiness of God’s presence.

verses.text: So Solomon overlaid the house within with pure gold. He drew chains of gold across before the inner sanctuary, and he overlaid it with gold.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon overlays the house inside with pure gold and hangs gold chains across the front of the inner sanctuary. Arminian readers see the gold as honoring God’s presence, and the chains as marking the boundary of the most holy place.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. The meaning of the chains is uncertain, and interpreters offer different explanations. Both traditions read the verse as showing the richness of the temple and the separation between the main hall and the inner sanctuary.

verses.text: He overlaid the whole house with gold, until all the house was finished. He also overlaid the whole altar that belonged to the inner sanctuary with gold.
verses.arminianNotes: He overlays the whole house with gold, along with the altar of the inner sanctuary. Arminians see the gold covering everything as expressing the glory due to God, with nothing in his house left plain or neglected.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that the altar here is probably the incense altar before the inner sanctuary. Both traditions read the verse as the climax of the interior description, highlighting the splendor of the place where God would dwell.
